title: Simon's problem: Theta(2^(n/2)) classical queries vs O(n) quantum queries
problem_statement: Given oracle access to f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1}^n with the promise that there is a nonzero s such that f(x) = f(y) iff y = x or y = x XOR s, find s.

input.parameter: n = number of input bits of f.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the 2^n-entry table only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical collision search
algorithms.idea: Query distinct random points until two values collide; the XOR of the colliding inputs is s.
algorithms.pseudocode: for x in random permutation: if f(x) seen at x': return x XOR x'
algorithms.correctness: Under the promise, f(x) = f(x') with x != x' implies x' = x XOR s.

algorithms.name: Simon's quantum algorithm
algorithms.idea: Each round (Hadamard, one query, Hadamard, measure) yields a uniformly random y with y.s = 0. About n rounds give n-1 independent equations, which Gaussian elimination over GF(2) solves for s.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n) queries: the expected number of rounds is E(n) = sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 1/(1 - 2^(-j)) = n - 1 + sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 1/(2^j - 1) < n + 0.6067 (the limit constant is the Erdős-Borwein constant 1.60669...); plus O(n^3) classical post-processing
algorithms.correctness: Simon 1997. After measuring the output register the input register is (|x0> + |x0 XOR s>)/sqrt(2); after H^n, the amplitude of y is proportional to 1 + (-1)^(y.s), so only y with y.s = 0 occur, uniformly.

relationship: Proven EXPONENTIAL separation in the query model: Omega(2^(n/2)) classical queries vs O(n) quantum queries. Historically the direct inspiration for Shor's factoring algorithm, which applies the same period-finding idea over Z_N.

sources.title: On the power of quantum computation
Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

verification.method: V1: both algorithms return s, independently checked against the promise structure of the table, for n = 1..10 (quantum, simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py using deferred measurement of the output register) and up to 16 (classical). V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle, averaged over random instances: classical fits 2^(n/2) and quantum fits n. Quantum counts are averaged over 40 instances per n. The exact expectation E(n) (see time_complexity) has log-log slope 1.019 against n over n = 2..10, so alpha near 1 is the expected outcome. Separately, the simulator's mean query count was compared with E(n) on 1500-4000 instances per n for n = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8: all within 1.3 standard errors (RESEARCH_LOG.md, 2026-10-06). Simulation time is exponential in n and is not the claim. Revised 2026-10-06 (RL-056): quantum n_values 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 with 100 instances per n (n = 2 dropped: its geometric spread dominated the fit, deviation analysis F5); the exact expectation E(n) has log-log slope 0.9573 against n over these values. Rivals: the quantum counts must reject 2^(n/2), the classical counts must reject n.

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle; it does not by itself imply BQP != BPP for explicit problems. The simulation never materialises the output register: lib.qsim.Oracle.apply_xor_and_measure_output samples the measured output value and collapses the input register, which is exact because the algorithm never touches the output register again.
notes: The cleanest proven exponential quantum-classical query separation, and the structural ancestor of Shor's algorithm (see staging/integer-factoring and staging/discrete-logarithm).
